text: CAST UDL Guidelines v2.2 (2018) — 3 principles (engagement / representation / action+expression), 9 guidelines, 31 checkpoints. Each principle maps to a neuroscience network (recognition / strategic / affective).
Paivio (1991) — dual-coding theory: separate but interconnected verbal + nonverbal (imagery) representations in memory. Foundational for visual-symbolic-verbal coordination in multimedia learning.

Mayer (ed.) Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning (2nd ed. 2014; 3rd ed. 2022). Canonical reference for the 12 multimedia-learning principles: coherence + redundancy + spatial/temporal contiguity + modality + multimedia + signaling + segmenting + pre-training + personalization + voice + image principles.

First comprehensive book-length presentation of UDL principles and practice since 2002, integrating a decade of CAST research on learner variability and the three networks (recognition, strategic, affective) underlying the three UDL principles.

Reflects on how the three UDL principles (multiple means of representation, expression, engagement) play out in an actual Harvard graduate-level course, with examples of course goals, materials, methods, and assessment redesigned via UDL.

Meta-analysis of 18 pre/post-test empirical studies (2013-2016) on UDL implementations; concludes UDL is effective for improving the learning process for all students but evidence on educational outcomes is not yet demonstrated.

Content analysis of 12 peer-reviewed empirical UDL papers (2012-2015); finds UDL research is in nascent stages with inconsistent operationalization of the framework and limited rigorous outcome evidence.

Documents the July 2024 Guidelines 3.0 release: shifts from educator- to learner-centered language, integrates asset-based pedagogies, centers learner identity and systemic barriers, and reframes the UDL goal as learner agency.

Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 peer-reviewed UDL studies (2015-2021) across six countries; reports statistically significant effects for student participants and specific-domain applications.

Systematic review of 20 studies (363 faculty, 5,293 students) on UDL faculty-training programs in higher ed; finds targeted UDL training increases teaching competence and supports inclusive pedagogical practice.

Defines 13 guidelines under POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) with 86 testable success criteria across A/AA/AAA conformance levels; adds 9 new criteria over 2.1 addressing focus appearance, target size, dragging movements, and cognitive accessibility.

Working draft of the next-generation accessibility standard with bronze/silver/gold conformance (replacing A/AA/AAA), broader scope to apps and emerging tech, and incorporation of usability testing and cognitive walkthroughs in higher conformance levels.

Introduces an eight-color qualitative palette (black, orange, sky blue, bluish green, yellow, blue, vermillion, reddish purple) selected to remain distinguishable under all three major forms of color vision deficiency; explicitly recommended by Nature journals.

Describes ColorBrewer, an evidence-based tool for selecting sequential, diverging, and qualitative map color schemes (3-12 classes) tuned for perceptual effectiveness, colorblind safety, photocopy reproduction, and display environment.

First eye-tracking study of font type on dyslexic reading (48 participants, 12 fonts); sans-serif, monospaced, and roman styles significantly outperform serif, proportional, and italic; specialized dyslexia fonts like OpenDyslexic are not faster than Arial or Helvetica.

Demonstrates in 54 Italian and 40 French dyslexic children that simply increasing inter-letter spacing (+18% body size) improves reading speed and accuracy on-the-fly without training, with no parallel benefit for typical readers.

Tests reading speed and accuracy with increased letter spacing, word spacing, and a dyslexia-targeted font in dyslexic and typical readers; finds no general advantage for any condition, partially contradicting Zorzi et al. (2012).

Describes MathPlayer, a browser plug-in that renders MathML visually and converts it to speech for screen readers (JAWS, Window-Eyes); supports synchronized highlighting, expression magnification, and Braille math output.

Documents MathJax 4 built-in accessibility: automatic speech-string generation injected via aria-label and aria-braillelabel, semantic enrichment for screen-reader accuracy, and an interactive expression explorer navigable via arrow keys after tab focus.

Examines five overload scenarios in multimedia learning and proposes one or two theory-based load-reduction techniques per scenario (off-loading, segmenting, pretraining, weeding, signaling, aligning, eliminating redundancy, synchronizing, individualizing), with empirical results testing each.

Two experiments show learners produce better retention and transfer when narration accompanies animation (modality effect) and when corresponding visual and verbal material is presented simultaneously (temporal-contiguity effect).

Summarizes 20 years of cognitive load theory evolution: distinguishes biologically primary vs. secondary knowledge, refines intrinsic/extraneous/germane load definitions, and sketches future directions for instructional-design research.

Concise review of CLT-derived methods to manage working-memory load during complex-task learning, covering worked examples, variability, segmenting, and modality with practical instructional implications.

Review of empirical work showing instructional techniques that benefit novices (e.g., worked examples, full explanations) can hinder more knowledgeable learners — what helps depends on prior expertise, so designs must fade scaffolds.
Meta-analysis of segmenting (chunking + user-paced) multimedia material; reports a positive overall effect on retention and transfer with moderators including learner control, pacing, and complexity.

Meta-analysis of 44 effect sizes from 29 experiments (N=2726) finds signaling cues produce a moderate positive effect on learning outcomes (d=0.38), moderated by study quality, prior-knowledge controls, and outcome reliability.

Meta-analytic synthesis of modality-effect experiments confirms learners perform better with spoken narration + graphics than printed text + graphics, with moderators around pacing, complexity, and system pacing.

Three studies show that analyzing contrasting cases first generates differentiated knowledge structures that prepare learners to benefit from a subsequent lecture or text — establishing the time-for-telling framework for sequencing.

Four 9th-grade statistics experiments show that invention activities (which appear inefficient on immediate tests) couple with subsequent lectures to produce strong transfer, procedural skill, and ability to evaluate data — operationalizing preparation for future learning.

Classroom study with 7th-grade math: students who first attempted ill-structured complex problems without scaffolds underperformed initially but outperformed direct-instruction peers on well-structured and transfer problems after subsequent instruction.

Articulates a two-phase generation-then-consolidation design (problem-solving before instruction) and reports three studies showing PF students outperformed direct-instruction peers on conceptual understanding and transfer at no cost to procedural fluency.

Meta-analysis of 53 studies / 166 comparisons (N>12,000) finds problem-solving-before-instruction yields significantly better conceptual understanding and transfer than instruction-first (d=0.36; up to 0.58 at high design fidelity), without compromising procedural knowledge.

Reviews PS-I research and proposes mechanisms by which initial problem-solving supports later instruction: activating prior knowledge, becoming aware of knowledge gaps, and noticing deep features — explaining when sequencing helps and when it does not.

Experiment shows that simply having students attempt problems before instruction is insufficient; benefits emerge only when the subsequent instruction explicitly builds on students typical erroneous solutions, making knowledge gaps salient.

30 single-case-design studies synthesized via Tau-BC meta-analysis show a large overall effect for CRA sequencing in math learning; moderator analysis weakly favors non-integrated (strictly sequential) over integrated CRA variants.

Dual coding theory (DCT) explains human behavior in terms of dynamic associative processes that operate on a rich network of modality-specific verbal and nonverbal (or imagery) representations; shows how DCT mechanisms can be used to model diverse educational phenomena.

First book to take a systematic dual-coding theoretical approach to all central issues of literacy — decoding, comprehension, memory in reading; planning, drafting, reviewing in writing — extending DCT to text-based learning.

Updates the Dual Coding Theory of mind, a theory of modern human cognition consisting of separate but interconnected nonverbal and verbal systems, and carefully compares DCT with contrasting single-code cognitive theories.

Reviews 1970s-90s research supporting that carefully constructed text illustrations enhance learners performance on text-dependent cognitive outcomes, and begins to systematically explore the whys, whens, and for-whoms of picture facilitation.

Experimental results are consistent with the physical-distinctiveness account and inconsistent with dual-coding theory as the explanation for the picture-superiority effect — i.e., picture advantage may be a distinctiveness phenomenon, not a dual-encoding one.

Manipulating physical distinctiveness of words eliminates the picture-superiority effect, supporting a distinctiveness-based rather than dual-coding-based mechanism for the picture advantage in recognition memory.

Introduces PRIMM (Predict-Run-Investigate-Modify-Make), building on Use-Modify-Create, levels of abstraction, and tracing/code-comprehension research — beginners focus on reading working code before writing their own.
Empirical study of teachers using PRIMM in school programming classrooms, reporting how the read-before-write structure affects lesson design and student talk about code.
Introduces the Use-Modify-Create progression — students first use existing computational artifacts, then modify them, then create their own — as a scaffold for developing computational thinking.

Subgoal-labeled worked examples for App Inventor programming significantly improved novice performance and transfer to novel tasks vs. unlabeled examples; supports structuring code-first exposition with explicit subgoals.

Studies the combined effect of subgoal labels, contextualization, and worked examples on novice computing problem-solving, finding worked-example + subgoal-label conditions outperform problem-solving practice.

Live coding — synchronously writing and executing code in front of students — is examined as a pedagogical technique that imparts skills like incremental development and debugging, with measured effects on novice programming learning.
Jupyter notebooks combine live re-executable code, narrative text, equations, and rich media into a single executable document — the canonical reference for notebook-as-medium.

Introduces reactive documents that embed live calculations alongside prose so readers can manipulate variables and see consequences — the design pattern underlying Observable, Tangle, and explorable-explanation pedagogy.
